title: U.S. House · Arizona's 5th District
area: East Valley suburbs of Phoenix, including parts of Mesa, Gilbert, Queen Creek, San Tan Valley, and Apache Junction.

context.text: This is an open seat. Incumbent Republican Andy Biggs, who had held the seat since 2017, did not seek re-election and instead ran for governor of Arizona. Elizabeth Lee won the July 21, 2026 Democratic primary with 64.5% of the vote over Chris James and Brian Hualde. Mark Lamb, the former Pinal County Sheriff (2017-2024) and 2024 U.S. Senate candidate, won the Republican primary with 58.6% over self-funded businessman Daniel Keenan, defeating candidates including state legislators Travis Grantham and Mike Gross for the nomination; Andy Biggs also withdrew from this primary. Lamb's primary win came amid public allegations from multiple women, reported by the Arizona Republic and independently verified by KTAR News, that he had sent them sexually charged messages and, in one case, threatened her with felony revenge-porn charges; Lamb largely declined to comment on the allegations, and in June 2026 a Pinal County Attorney's Office review concluded it found 'no evidence that Lamb acted in a criminal manner.' Cook Political Report rated the district R+10.

candidates.name: Elizabeth Lee
candidates.ballotNote: Won the July 21, 2026 Democratic primary with 64.5% of the vote

summary.text: Elizabeth Lee is the Democratic nominee for Arizona's 5th Congressional District, an open seat. She is a registered nurse who describes herself as a board-certified reproductive health and infertility nurse and patient advocate, and has worked as a nurse, consultant and healthcare advocate. She won the July 21, 2026 Democratic primary with 66.0 percent of the vote and says she is running to be the first woman to represent the district, with healthcare as a central theme.

background.text: Earned a high school diploma from Dover High School, a bachelor's degree from Northwestern State University in 2005, and an associate degree from the Carrington College of Nursing in 2013.
Says she grew up battling an undiagnosed illness for years, which she says shaped her decision to become a nurse and patient advocate.
background.quote: I grew up battling a mysterious illness that went undiagnosed for years, and it was only after becoming a nurse that I began to crack my own medical mystery.

background.text: Describes herself as a board-certified Reproductive Health and Infertility Nurse and a board-certified Patient Advocate, and says she is a product of public schools.
Career experience includes working as a nurse, consultant, and healthcare advocate.

Has been affiliated with the American Society for Reproductive Medicine, the ASRM Center for Policy Leadership, the Pacific Coast Reproductive Society, Reproductive Freedom for All, RESOLVE: The National Infertility Association, and the Arizona State Board of Nursing.
Won the July 21, 2026 Democratic primary for U.S. House Arizona District 5, defeating Chris James and Brian Hualde with 66.0 percent of the vote (30,857 votes).
In her Ballotpedia survey, describes herself as a nurse, patient advocate, and mom running to be the first woman to represent Arizona's 5th Congressional District.
Endorsed by Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D), state Sen. Analise Ortiz (D), and Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes (D), among other groups.

priorities.text: Healthcare as a human right, citing her nursing background and work with families facing infertility and other medical crises, pledging to fight so 'no one is left behind, no child denied care and no family bankrupted for the right to live.'
priorities.quote: In Washington I will fight to guarantee that no one is left behind, no child denied care and no family bankrupted for the right to live.

priorities.text: Increasing public school funding, opposing the diversion of taxpayer dollars to private schools she says face little transparency or accountability.
priorities.quote: Public dollars belong in public schools, and I will fight in Washington to ensure Arizona invests in its students instead of subsidizing unregulated private institutions.

priorities.text: Addressing the housing affordability crisis by curbing corporate control of real estate.
priorities.quote: In Washington I will fight to curb corporate control of real estate and put the dream of safe, affordable housing back within reach for Arizona families.

positions.summary: Says healthcare is a human right and pledges to fight so that no patient is denied care or bankrupted by medical costs, drawing on her career as a reproductive-health nurse and patient advocate.
Opposes directing public education dollars to private schools, saying 'public dollars belong in public schools.'
positions.quote: Public dollars belong in public schools, and I will fight in Washington to ensure Arizona invests in its students instead of subsidizing unregulated private institutions.

positions.summary: Says she will fight to curb corporate control of the real-estate market to make housing more affordable for Arizona families.

candidates.name: Mark Lamb
candidates.ballotNote: Won the July 21, 2026 Republican primary with 58.6% of the vote, endorsed by President Trump

summary.text: Mark Lamb is the Republican nominee for Arizona's 5th Congressional District, an open seat. A former law enforcement officer, he was Pinal County sheriff from 2017 to 2024 and ran unsuccessfully in the 2024 Republican U.S. Senate primary, losing to Kari Lake. He won the July 21, 2026 Republican primary with the endorsement of President Donald Trump and Turning Point USA, amid public allegations from multiple women that he sent them sexually charged messages; a Pinal County Attorney's Office review concluded it found no evidence of criminal conduct. His campaign has denied the allegations.

background.text: Born in Hawaii in 1972 and spent much of his childhood there, with periods in Arizona, the Philippines, Panama and Argentina; graduated from Chandler High School in Arizona.
Before law enforcement, started a paintball business in Utah and later worked in pest control; moved back to Arizona in 2003.
Worked for the police department of the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community for six years before joining the Pinal County Sheriff's Office in 2012.
Elected Sheriff of Pinal County in 2016 to succeed Paul Babeu, and re-elected unopposed in 2020, serving from January 2017 to December 2024.

Appeared on the television series Live PD and hosted its spinoff Live PD: Wanted, and was featured in Season 5 of 60 Days In; is the author of the self-published book American Sheriff: Traditional Values in a Modern World.
Co-founded Protect America Now, a coalition of sheriffs, in February 2021.
Ran for U.S. Senate in 2024 to succeed Kyrsten Sinema, and was defeated in the Republican primary by Kari Lake.

Entered the Republican primary for Arizona's 5th District in October 2025 after Rep. Andy Biggs chose not to seek re-election; won the July 21, 2026 primary over Daniel Keenan, 58.7 percent to 41.3 percent.

In May and June 2026, news reports said multiple women alleged that Lamb sent them sexually charged messages. On June 22, 2026, Pinal County Attorney Brad Miller's preliminary review found no evidence that Lamb acted in a criminal manner, and the matter was closed; Lamb's campaign has denied the allegations.

priorities.text: Campaigns on a platform of traditional values, describing a need for what news coverage characterized as a 'national revival of faith, family, freedom,' while denouncing what he calls 'America's moral decay.'

record.text: Multiple women alleged, in an Arizona Republic investigation independently verified by KTAR News, that Lamb sent them explicit photos and sexually charged messages from his personal phone and campaign accounts while serving as sheriff; one woman said he threatened her with felony revenge-porn charges. Lamb largely declined to comment on the allegations; his wife called the reports a 'massive smear campaign' in a Facebook post. In June 2026, Pinal County Attorney Brad Miller concluded a review of the matter, finding 'no evidence that Lamb acted in a criminal manner.'

The American Sheriff Foundation, a charity Lamb established in 2018 that raised more than $50,000 in its first year, left at least $18,000 in spending unaccounted for on tax filings, the Arizona Republic reported in 2020. The IRS revoked its tax-exempt status in 2021 for failing to file required reports, and Arizona moved to administratively dissolve it in 2024 after it also failed to file required state annual reports.
